cards.title: 4.1 Exponential Functions
body: 4.1 Exponential Functions

**Definition:** An **Exponential Function** is a function of the form $$f(x) = a^x$$, where the base $$a$$ is a positive constant other than one ($$a > 0$$ and $$a \neq 1$$), and the exponent $$x$$ is any real number.

### Deep Dive
Exponential functions represent one of the most powerful mathematical structures used to model rapid, non-linear change. Unlike polynomial functions where the base is a variable and the exponent is constant (such as $$f(x) = x^2$$), exponential functions feature a constant base raised to a variable exponent. This structural inversion results in a completely different growth profile. While polynomial curves grow at a predictable, polynomial rate, exponential curves grow at an accelerating rate that quickly surpasses any polynomial curve of any degree.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body: The domain of any basic exponential function is the set of all real numbers, $$(-\infty, \infty)$$, meaning we can substitute any real value for $$x$$. The range, however, is strictly positive real numbers, $$(0, \infty)$$, because a positive base raised to any real power can never yield a negative number or zero. Every unreflected and unshifted exponential graph of the form $$y = a^x$$ passes through the coordinate $$(0, 1)$$, which is its y-intercept.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body:
| Function Type | Base Condition | Graphical Behavior | Horizontal Asymptote |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Exponential Growth** | $$a > 1$$ | Curves upward from left to right | $$y = 0$$ (as $$x \to -\infty$$) |
| **Exponential Decay** | $$0 < a < 1$$ | Curves downward from left to right | $$y = 0$$ (as $$x \to \infty$$) |
| **Vertically Shifted** | $$a > 1, k \neq 0$$ | Curves upward, shifted vertically | $$y = k$$ (as $$x \to -\infty$$) |

> **💡 Did You Know?**: If you fold a standard piece of paper in half 42 times, its thickness will double exponentially until it exceeds the distance from the Earth to the Moon! This is a physical demonstration of the power of exponential growth.

body: logarithmic function is equal to the domain of the exponential function. Therefore, the domain of $$f(x) = \log_a(x)$$ is strictly restricted to positive numbers, $$x > 0$$ (or $$(0, \infty)$$), meaning you cannot take the logarithm of a negative number or zero. The range, however, is unrestricted, covering all real numbers, $$(-\infty, \infty)$$.

Graphically, the inverse relationship is represented by a reflection across the diagonal identity line $$y = x$$. While the exponential graph has a horizontal asymptote at $$y = 0$$ and a y-intercept at $$(0, 1)$$, the logarithmic graph has a **vertical asymptote** at $$x = 0$$ (the y-axis) and an x-intercept at $$(1, 0)$$. If $$a > 1$$, the graph rises slowly from left to right; if $$0 < a < 1$$, the graph falls slowly.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body: By introducing transformation parameters, we write the general form as $$f(x) = c \cdot a^{x - h} + k$$. Here, $$h$$ represents a horizontal translation, $$k$$ represents a vertical translation, and $$c$$ acts as a vertical stretch or reflection factor. The vertical shift $$k$$ is especially important because it shifts the horizontal asymptote of the graph to the line $$y = k$$, changing the range of the function to $$(k, \infty)$$ if $$c > 0$$.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body:
To simplify and manipulate logarithmic expressions, we rely on three primary properties derived from the laws of exponents:
1. **Product Rule:** $$\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y$$
2. **Quotient Rule:** $$\log_a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \log_a x - \log_a y$$
3. **Power Rule:** $$\log_a(x^p) = p \log_a x$$
These properties allow us to expand complex expressions into simpler terms or condense multiple logarithmic terms into a single expression, which is essential for solving equations.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body: Graphically, exponential functions are split into two categories based on the value of $$a$$. If $$a > 1$$, the function models **exponential growth**, curving upward from left to right. As $$x$$ approaches negative infinity, the curve gets closer and closer to the x-axis, making the line $$y = 0$$ a **horizontal asymptote**. If $$0 < a < 1$$, the function models **exponential decay**, curving downward from left to right. In this case, the horizontal asymptote $$y = 0$$ is approached as $$x$$ goes to positive infinity.

cards.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
body: To solve basic exponential equations algebraically, we rely on the one-to-one property of exponential functions: if the bases match, their exponents must be equal ($$a^u = a^v \iff u = v$$). For example, to solve $$32^{x+1} = 128$$, we rewrite both sides using a base of $$2$$: $$(2^5)^{x+1} = 2^7$$, which simplifies to the linear equation $$5x + 5 = 7$$, giving a solution of $$x = 0.4$$. This technique is highly effective when the bases can be matched.

cards.title: 4.2 Logarithmic Functions
body: 4.2 Logarithmic Functions

**Definition:** A **Logarithmic Function** is the inverse of an exponential function. It is written as $$f(x) = \log_a(x)$$, where $$x > 0$$, the base $$a > 0$$, and $$a \neq 1$$. The relationship is defined by: $$y = \log_a(x) \iff a^y = x$$.

### Deep Dive
Logarithmic functions were developed to invert the operations of exponential functions. A logarithm is simply an answer to the question: "To what power must I raise the base $$a$$ to get $$x$$?" Because exponentials and logarithms are inverses, they share a symmetric relationship. Swapping the inputs and outputs of the exponential function $$y = a^x$$ yields the logarithmic relationship $$x = a^y$$, which we write in logarithmic form as $$y = \log_a(x)$$.

body: Most scientific calculators only contain buttons for the **common logarithm** (base 10, written as $$\log x$$) and the **natural logarithm** (base $$e$$, written as $$\ln x$$). To calculate logarithms with other bases, we use the **Change of Base Formula**: $$\log_b m = \frac{\log_a m}{\log_a b}$$. This formula allows us to convert any logarithm into a ratio of common or natural logarithms, making it easy to evaluate numerically.
